Option C — Materialize as an incremental model partitioned by account_created_month with `incremental_strategy = 'insert_overwrite'`. Retroactive corrections trigger a partition-level overwrite of the affected months. Daily runs overwrite only the current month's partition.

Option D — Keep as a view but add a downstream materialized summary table (pre-aggregated by stage, cohort_month, and account_tier) refreshed nightly. Analysts query the summary for funnel metrics; the view is used only for ad-hoc deep dives on specific accounts.
explanation:
Option B is correct. For a funnel model where each account has exactly one current state (unique_key = 'account_id'), an incremental merge strategy is the right design. On each daily run, only accounts with CRM updated_at > last_run_timestamp are processed and merged — this satisfies requirement 3 (efficient daily updates). The merge on account_id correctly handles retroactive CRM corrections: when a CRM correction changes an account's stage history, the updated_at timestamp advances, causing that account to be included in the next incremental run, and the merge overwrites the previous row. Requirement 2 (backfill support) is satisfied by the --full-refresh flag, which forces a full table rebuild from source. Requirement 1 (sub-10-second queries) is satisfied by the pre-materialized table replacing the 90-second view.

Option A (full refresh daily + delta model) is operationally complex: maintaining two separate models (a full-refresh 'base' and an incremental 'delta') for one logical entity creates synchronization risk. If the delta model's updated_at filter misses any account (e.g., due to CRM timestamp lag), that account's state becomes stale in production. A single incremental model with a well-defined watermark is simpler and more reliable.

Option C (partition by account_created_month with insert_overwrite) is a reasonable pattern for event tables but poorly suited to entity-state tables like a funnel model. Account stage can change at any time regardless of when the account was created — a correction to a 2-year-old account triggers a full partition overwrite of the month the account was created, which may contain thousands of other accounts that don't need reprocessing. This introduces unnecessary recomputation and partition management complexity.

Option D (view + downstream summary) partially addresses requirement 1 for aggregated metrics but fails requirements 2 and 3 for ad-hoc account-level queries. The 90-second view performance problem is only deferred, not solved — any query that needs account-level funnel detail (e.g., 'show me all accounts in the Trial stage for more than 30 days') still hits the slow view. And retroactive backfills are not addressed at all since the view always computes from source.
hints: Consider which incremental strategy correctly handles retroactive CRM corrections — the key is whether corrected records will be re-processed on the next incremental run.

A merge strategy on a unique entity key (account_id) naturally handles both new accounts and corrections to existing accounts in a single incremental run — evaluate whether this satisfies all three requirements.

The --full-refresh flag in dbt provides a built-in backfill mechanism for incremental models — consider whether a separate 'delta model' is needed or whether a single incremental model with --full-refresh support is sufficient.

title: Wide One-Big-Table vs. Normalized Model for High-Cardinality Real-Time Analytics
scenario_context: A logistics company is building an operational analytics platform serving three teams: (1) operations analysts who query shipment status, ETA, carrier, and customer info together in ad-hoc slices, (2) an ML team that needs all features for a delay prediction model refreshed every 15 minutes, and (3) a billing team that needs carrier cost and contractual rate joined with shipment weight and zone for invoice generation. The data is stored in a cloud data warehouse. A senior engineer proposes a single wide OBT pre-joining all shipment attributes (100+ columns) refreshed every 15 minutes. Another proposes normalized intermediate models (shipments, carriers, customers, zones) joined in a final mart view per use case.
description: Which modeling approach best serves the three teams' differing latency, freshness, and column-access requirements at scale?
options: Option A — Normalized intermediate models materialized as tables (shipments, carriers, customers, zones), each refreshed on its own cadence. Team-specific mart views join the tables needed for each use case. The OBT for the ML team is a separate scheduled model joining all intermediate tables, refreshed every 15 minutes.

Option B — A single wide OBT (100+ columns) refreshed every 15 minutes as a full materialized table. All three teams query the same table; column pruning in the BI and ML layers limits unnecessary data transfer. Billing and operations teams use column-specific SELECT statements.

Option C — Two OBTs: an operational OBT (shipment status, ETA, carrier, customer) refreshed every 15 minutes for operations and ML, and a financial OBT (carrier cost, rate, weight, zone) refreshed nightly for billing. Billing can tolerate daily freshness; operations cannot.

Option D — Normalized intermediate models as views (not materialized), with a single wide OBT materialized as the only table. Intermediate models provide lineage clarity; the OBT provides query performance. All teams query the OBT exclusively.
explanation:
Option A is correct. The three teams have fundamentally different access patterns: operations needs ad-hoc multi-dimensional slices (variable column access), the ML team needs a wide feature set refreshed frequently, and billing needs a narrow financial join refreshed daily. Normalized intermediate models materialized as tables — each refreshed at its own cadence — allow each team's mart to be right-sized for its access pattern. The ML team's OBT is a purpose-built scheduled model that joins all intermediate tables on its 15-minute cadence without burdening the other marts. Operations' mart view joins only the shipment, carrier, and customer tables. Billing's mart joins only carrier and zone tables, refreshed nightly. This design minimizes unnecessary recomputation and gives each team a table optimized for their queries.

Option B (single wide OBT, 100+ columns) fails for three reasons: (1) a 100+ column table refreshed every 15 minutes as a full materialized table is extremely expensive in a cloud warehouse billed by data scanned — operations and billing queries that need 10–15 columns pay for scanning 100+ columns; (2) a single refresh cadence (15 minutes) is unnecessarily expensive for billing, which only needs daily freshness; (3) a monolithic OBT is fragile — a schema change for the ML feature set affects all three teams simultaneously.

Option C (two OBTs) is a reasonable compromise but creates a misalignment: the ML team needs a wide feature set that includes financial attributes (carrier cost, zone) for its delay prediction model. The financial OBT is refreshed nightly, so the ML team cannot use it for its 15-minute feature refresh. The two-OBT design forces a choice between wide features for ML and the billing freshness requirement.

Option D (intermediate views + wide OBT) defeats the purpose of intermediate models by making them views. View chains in complex join scenarios don't benefit from the performance of materialized intermediate tables — the query engine must still execute all joins from source on every query. The single wide OBT then becomes the only materialized layer, which has the same problems as Option B.
hints: Three teams with different column-access patterns, freshness requirements, and query volumes are unlikely to be best served by a single wide table — consider whether a single OBT's refresh cadence and column count can be right-sized for all three simultaneously.

Materializing intermediate normalized models as tables (not views) allows each team's mart to join only the tables it needs, at the cadence it requires — without coupling all teams to a single monolithic refresh.

The ML team's need for a wide feature set at 15-minute freshness is a specific use case that can be served by a dedicated scheduled OBT built from the normalized intermediate tables — it doesn't require all teams to share that wide table.

title: Modeling Requirements for a Multi-Currency Financial Reporting System
scenario_context: A multinational e-commerce company sells in 40 currencies. Finance requires: (1) all revenue reported in local transaction currency for VAT compliance, (2) all revenue converted to USD at the exchange rate effective on the transaction date for consolidated P&L, (3) monthly exchange rate snapshots for planning scenarios (e.g., 'what would this month's revenue be at last month's average rate?'). The current orders fact table stores transaction amounts in local currency only. A data architect proposes adding a USD_amount column to the fact table, populated by a nightly lookup against an exchange_rate table. Another proposes a separate currency_conversion_fact at the grain of (transaction_id, target_currency, rate_date).
description: Which dimensional schema correctly models multi-currency financial reporting while satisfying VAT compliance, consolidated P&L, and planning scenario requirements?
options: Option A — Keep the orders fact table with local_currency_amount and local_currency_code columns only. Add an exchange_rate_dim at the grain of (currency_pair, rate_date) containing the daily exchange rate. USD P&L queries join fact to rate_dim on (currency_code, transaction_date); planning scenarios join on a different rate_date. This preserves the single-source-of-truth for amounts and externalizes conversion logic.

Option B — Add a usd_amount column to the orders fact table, populated nightly by multiplying local_currency_amount by the exchange rate on transaction_date. Add a usd_planning_amount column populated using last month's average rate. VAT compliance queries use local_currency_amount; P&L queries use usd_amount; planning uses usd_planning_amount.

Option C — Add a usd_amount column to the fact table for the primary consolidated view. Build a planning_scenario_dim that contains scenario exchange rates (last_month_avg, ytd_avg, budget_rate). Planning queries join the fact to the scenario dim and multiply local_currency_amount by the scenario rate at query time. VAT queries use local_currency_amount.

Option D — Build a currency_conversion_fact at the grain of (transaction_id, target_currency, rate_date), pre-computing all currency combinations for every transaction. USD P&L, EUR reporting, and GBP reporting each read from this table filtered by target_currency. Planning scenarios use a different rate_date.
explanation:
Option A is correct. The fundamental principle of multi-currency dimensional modeling is to store amounts in local (transaction) currency as the atomic fact, and to externalize the conversion rate as a separate dimension. This design: (1) satisfies VAT compliance — local_currency_amount is always the source of truth, never derived; (2) satisfies P&L — a query-time join to exchange_rate_dim on (currency_code, transaction_date) produces the correct historical USD amount at the rate effective on the transaction date; (3) satisfies planning scenarios — the same fact table joined to exchange_rate_dim on a different rate_date (e.g., last month's average rate) produces alternative-rate revenue figures. No amounts in the fact table ever change when exchange rates are revised; only the rate dimension is updated.

Option B (multiple pre-computed amount columns) embeds conversion logic and specific exchange rate choices into the fact table at load time. The critical problem: if the source exchange rate is corrected (rates are frequently revised after initial publication), all historical usd_amount and usd_planning_amount values in the fact table must be reprocessed. Adding a new planning scenario (e.g., budget rate for next year) requires an ETL change and a new column. This design is brittle and expensive to maintain at 40-currency scale.

Option C is a clever compromise: store only local_currency_amount and compute USD conversions at query time using a planning_scenario_dim. This avoids the reprocessing problem of Option B and correctly handles planning scenarios. However, computing currency conversion at query time (local_amount × scenario_rate) for every row in a large orders fact table is expensive, particularly for consolidated P&L queries that must aggregate millions of transactions in 40 different currencies. For a consolidated P&L workload that runs frequently, pre-joining to the rate dim and pre-aggregating in a mart model (building on Option A's foundation) is more practical.

Option D (currency_conversion_fact with all combinations) pre-computes too many rows: transaction_count × target_currency_count × relevant_rate_dates. For a company with 1M daily transactions in 40 currencies and multiple rate scenarios, this table grows extremely quickly. It also conflates the transaction fact (an event) with a derived calculation (a conversion), making the data model harder to understand and govern. The correct pattern is to compute conversions in a mart or reporting layer by joining to the rate dimension, not to pre-materialize all combinations in a second fact table.
hints: In multi-currency modeling, the atomic fact should always be the local transaction currency — conversion to reporting currency should be a join to a rate table, not a pre-computed column in the fact.
Pre-computing converted amounts in the fact table creates a dependency between the fact table and exchange rates — consider what happens when historical rates are revised.

A rate dimension at the grain of (currency_pair, rate_date) allows any target currency and any historical or scenario rate to be applied at query time without changing the fact table — evaluate this against each of the three stated requirements.

title: Bi-Temporal Pricing History for Backdated Corrections
scenario_context: A B2B SaaS company maintains a contract_prices table in Snowflake tracking the negotiated monthly price for each enterprise customer. Prices change infrequently but are sometimes corrected retroactively — for example, a price agreed on March 1 at $500/month might be discovered to be incorrect and corrected to $450/month on March 20, with the effective date backdated to March 1. Finance has two distinct, non-negotiable reporting requirements: (1) valid-time queries — 'what price was contractually active for customer X on business date D?' used for billing reconciliation; (2) transaction-time queries — 'what did our system hold for customer X's price as of system date D?' used when regulators ask what was reported in a March 15 monthly statement. The table currently holds roughly 8,000 active contracts; corrections occur on approximately 5% of contracts per month.
description: Which design cleanly satisfies both reporting requirements as backdated corrections accumulate over time?
options: Option A — Bi-temporal table: add four date columns — valid_from and valid_to for the business-time axis, and recorded_from and recorded_to for the system-time axis. When a correction arrives on March 20: close recorded_to = March 20 on the original row and insert a corrected row with the corrected price, valid_from = March 1, and recorded_from = March 20. Both query types become simple date-range predicates on indexed columns.

Option B — SCD Type 2 with a correction_flag BOOLEAN and correction_applied_at TIMESTAMP. Original rows are retained; corrections add new rows with the corrected valid_from and the flag set to true. Transaction-time queries reconstruct system state by scanning rows where correction_applied_at is on or before the as-of system date and applying a ROW_NUMBER() window to find the latest belief per customer.

Option C — Two separate tables: contract_prices (SCD Type 2, manages valid time only) and price_audit_log (append-only copy of every row version with a logged_at timestamp). Valid-time queries use contract_prices; audit queries use price_audit_log. Each table is managed independently.

Option D — Append-only event log: every price change or correction is a new row with (customer_id, price, valid_from, event_timestamp). No rows are ever updated or closed. Both query types reconstruct state by applying a ROW_NUMBER() over event_timestamp and filtering on valid_from, keeping only the most recent event for each valid range as of the desired system date.
explanation:
Option A is correct. Bi-temporal modeling adds two independent time axes as first-class columns: business (valid) time and system (transaction) time. When a backdated correction arrives, the original row's recorded_to is closed and a corrected row is inserted — the original is never deleted. This means the table always contains the full correction history. Both query types reduce to a two-predicate range scan: WHERE :business_date BETWEEN valid_from AND valid_to AND '9999-12-31' = recorded_to for the current system view, or WHERE :business_date BETWEEN valid_from AND valid_to AND :system_date BETWEEN recorded_from AND recorded_to for a historical system snapshot. No reconstruction, no flag scanning, no cross-table joins — both predicates land on indexed columns.

Option B is a common half-measure. The correction_flag + correction_applied_at approach can record that a correction happened and when, but it cannot cleanly reconstruct what the system held at an arbitrary past point in time when multiple corrections have accumulated. If three corrections have been applied to one customer over six months, finding the system state on any specific date requires scanning all rows, ordering by correction_applied_at, and evaluating overlapping valid ranges in code — none of which is a simple index scan. The design conflates both time axes into a single ordered row stream with no physical separation between 'when the business fact was true' and 'when the system believed it.'

Option C correctly identifies that two concerns need two stores, but physical separation creates a synchronization risk: if the write to contract_prices succeeds but the corresponding write to price_audit_log fails (network blip, transaction boundary mismatch), the audit trail is silently incomplete. The cross-table join for queries that need both axes is also non-trivial — the dimension evolves via SCD Type 2 while the audit log is append-only, so schemas can drift. This pattern is common in practice as an engineering approximation, but it is not a coherent model: there is no single table that correctly answers either query type alone, and the combination adds operational fragility.

Option D (append-only event log) is architecturally sound for immutable stores but imposes reconstructive complexity on every consumer. A ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY event_timestamp) computed at query time is expensive and error-prone in an OLAP warehouse used by analysts who write ad-hoc SQL. The design also has an ambiguity: if multiple events exist for the same customer with overlapping valid ranges (an original and a correction, both starting March 1), determining which one was 'current' as of a past system date requires careful event-ordering logic that belongs in the ETL layer, not in every analyst query.
hints: Standard history-tracking patterns record when a fact was true in the business world. But if a correction is applied retroactively, that pattern can't tell you what the system believed *before* the correction. Which design preserves both time dimensions independently?

When a backdated correction is applied on March 20 with effective date March 1, two independent dates are in play: the date the business fact became true (March 1) and the date the system learned about it (March 20). Both need to be independently queryable without reconstruction.

A bi-temporal table answers both query types with simple range predicates on indexed date columns — WHERE :date BETWEEN valid_from AND valid_to for business time, and WHERE :date BETWEEN recorded_from AND recorded_to for system time. If a design requires ROW_NUMBER() or a cross-table join to answer either query, it is not truly bi-temporal.

title: Bi-Temporal Queries: Correct Predicates for Both Time Axes
scenario_context:
A pricing table uses bi-temporal modeling with four date columns:
  valid_from    DATE  -- when the price became contractually effective
  valid_to      DATE  -- when the price ceased to be contractually effective (9999-12-31 = currently valid)
  recorded_from DATE  -- when the system first recorded this row
  recorded_to   DATE  -- when this row was superseded in the system (9999-12-31 = currently recorded)

Row history for customer X:
  Row 1: price=$500, valid_from=2024-03-01, valid_to=9999-12-31, recorded_from=2024-03-01, recorded_to=2024-03-20
  Row 2: price=$450, valid_from=2024-03-01, valid_to=9999-12-31, recorded_from=2024-03-20, recorded_to=9999-12-31
  (On March 20, the system corrected the March 1 price from $500 to $450 retroactively)
description: A regulator asks: 'What price did your system report for customer X on March 15?' (transaction-time query). A billing team asks: 'What is the currently active price for customer X?' (current valid-time query). Which pair of SQL predicates correctly answers each question?
options: Regulator (transaction-time, March 15): WHERE '2024-03-15' BETWEEN recorded_from AND recorded_to — returns Row 1 ($500, the price the system held on March 15 before the correction); Billing (current valid-time): WHERE valid_to = '9999-12-31' AND recorded_to = '9999-12-31' — returns Row 2 ($450, the current corrected price)

Regulator: WHERE valid_from <= '2024-03-15' AND valid_to >= '2024-03-15' — returns the price valid on March 15 in business time; Billing: WHERE recorded_to = '9999-12-31' — returns the latest recorded row regardless of its validity period

Regulator: WHERE recorded_from = '2024-03-15' — returns the row first recorded on that exact date; Billing: WHERE valid_from = (SELECT MAX(valid_from) FROM prices WHERE customer_id = X) — returns the most recently effective price

Both queries use the same predicate: WHERE valid_from <= :date AND valid_to >= :date — the valid_from/valid_to axis captures both the business fact and when the system knew about it, because corrections update valid_from retroactively
explanation:
Option A is correct. Bi-temporal modeling has two independent time axes:

**Transaction-time (system time):** What did the system hold on a given date? Predicate: `WHERE :system_date BETWEEN recorded_from AND recorded_to`. On March 15, Row 1 is the active system row (recorded_from=Mar 1, recorded_to=Mar 20). BETWEEN returns Row 1 → price $500. This is what was reported in March 15 statements, invoices, or regulatory filings.

**Valid-time (business time, current):** What is the currently known price for customer X? Both axes must be currently open: `WHERE valid_to = '9999-12-31' AND recorded_to = '9999-12-31'`. Returns Row 2 → price $450 (the corrected price, currently valid, currently recorded).

Option B mixes the axes. The regulator predicate filters on valid_from/valid_to (business time), which returns the price *contractually* active on March 15 — that is Row 2 ($450, backdated to March 1). But the regulator is asking what the *system reported* on March 15, which was $500 before the correction. These are different questions.

Option C uses an equality predicate on recorded_from — no row was created on March 15 (they were created March 1 and March 20), so this returns zero rows.

Option D collapses both axes into one, which is the definition of a non-bi-temporal design. A backdated correction setting valid_from=March 1 for Row 2 would make it appear as if $450 was always known since March 1 — erasing the record that the system ever held $500.
hints: Transaction-time asks 'what did the system believe?' — which columns track when the system created/closed each row?
Valid-time asks 'what is the business fact?' — which columns track when the business contract was active?
For a current valid-time query, both time axes must be open-ended (9999-12-31). Why do you need both conditions, not just one?

title: Cross-Hierarchy Reporting: Two Hierarchies in One Dimension
scenario_context:
A retailer has dim_product with products in two independent hierarchies:
  - Merchandise hierarchy: product → subcategory → category → department
  - Finance hierarchy: product → cost_center → division → region

Analysts need to report: 'Top 3 products by revenue within each department AND within each division in the same query.' Both hierarchies must be navigable independently.

Current design uses two separate dimension tables (dim_product_merch, dim_product_finance) joined to fact_sales via product_id.
description: Which design supports efficient cross-hierarchy reporting in a single query without row multiplication?
options: Consolidate both hierarchies as flat columns in a single dim_product table (department, category, subcategory, division, cost_center, region as direct product attributes); use RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY revenue DESC) and RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY division ORDER BY revenue DESC) in one query against the single dimension
Keep the two separate dimension tables and join both to fact_sales; use UNION ALL to combine department-level and division-level results with a hierarchy_type column to distinguish them
Build role-playing dimensions where dim_product_merch and dim_product_finance are views of the same base table filtered by a hierarchy_type flag; join both views to fact_sales with different aliases

Use a bridge table (bridge_product_hierarchy) with columns (product_id, hierarchy_type, level_name, level_value) and join fact_sales through the bridge — one row per (product, hierarchy level), allowing arbitrary hierarchy traversal
explanation:
Option A is correct for standard dimensional modeling of multiple fixed hierarchies on the same dimension. Storing all hierarchy levels as flat, denormalized attributes on each product row enables cross-hierarchy reporting in a single join (fact_sales → dim_product) without row multiplication:

```sql
SELECT product_name, department, division, revenue,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS dept_rank,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY division ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS div_rank
FROM fact_sales fs JOIN dim_product dp USING (product_id)
```

Filtering `WHERE dept_rank <= 3 OR div_rank <= 3` returns top-3 in either hierarchy in one pass. Each fact_sales row joins to exactly one dim_product row — no multiplication.

Option B (UNION ALL of two separate joins) joins fact_sales twice and unions the results, producing 2× the I/O and compute. Window function ranking must happen after the union, complicating the query.

Option C (role-playing dimension) is for the same dimension playing *different roles* in one query (e.g., ship_date vs order_date from dim_date), not for two different hierarchies on the same entity. It does not simplify the join.

Option D (bridge table for hierarchy traversal) is appropriate for variable-depth hierarchies (e.g., org charts with unlimited depth), but it introduces one row per hierarchy level per product, multiplying rows during joins and requiring careful DISTINCT or pre-aggregation. It is over-engineered for fixed, known hierarchy levels.
hints: If each product belongs to exactly one position in each hierarchy, can you store all hierarchy-level attributes as simple columns on the product row?
Joining fact_sales to one dim_product with all hierarchy columns vs. joining to two separate dimension tables — which approach produces one fact row per join, and which produces multiple?

title: Fact-to-Fact Join: Avoiding Fan-Out Row Multiplication
scenario_context:
A data warehouse has two fact tables:
  fact_orders: 50M rows — (order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_revenue)
  fact_support_tickets: 8M rows — (ticket_id, customer_id, created_date, resolution_days)

An analyst writes:

```sql
SELECT
  fo.customer_id,
  SUM(fo.order_revenue) AS total_revenue,
  AVG(fst.resolution_days) AS avg_resolution
FROM fact_orders fo
JOIN fact_support_tickets fst ON fo.customer_id = fst.customer_id
WHERE YEAR(fo.order_date) = 2024
  AND YEAR(fst.created_date) = 2024
GROUP BY fo.customer_id
```

The query produces revenue figures 3–15× higher than expected for some customers.
description: What causes the inflated revenue, and how should the query be rewritten?
options: The join of two fact tables on customer_id produces a cross product per customer: a customer with 10 orders and 5 tickets generates 50 joined rows — each order is repeated once per matching ticket, so SUM(order_revenue) counts each order's revenue 5 times; fix by pre-aggregating each fact in a CTE before joining on customer_id

The inflation is caused by the WHERE clause filtering on two different date columns — SQL applies only the first predicate when filtering on separate tables; fix by splitting into two subqueries filtered independently

AVG(fst.resolution_days) over a joined result set incorrectly averages over duplicated rows — use MEDIAN(fst.resolution_days) instead, which is resistant to duplication artifacts in fact-to-fact joins
The join key (customer_id) is not selective enough — use a more granular key like (customer_id, order_date) and add a date-range condition in the join predicate to prevent row multiplication
explanation:
Joining two fact tables through a shared dimension key produces a Cartesian product within each key group — the classic fan-out problem. For a customer with 10 orders and 5 support tickets, the JOIN produces 10 × 5 = 50 rows. `SUM(order_revenue)` then sums each order's revenue 5 times, inflating the result by 5×. The inflation factor equals the number of matching rows in the other fact table, which varies per customer — hence the 3–15× range.

Correct approach — pre-aggregate each fact independently in CTEs:

```sql
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(order_revenue) AS total_revenue
    FROM fact_orders
    WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
ticket_stats AS (
    SELECT customer_id, AVG(resolution_days) AS avg_resolution
    FROM fact_support_tickets
    WHERE YEAR(created_date) = 2024
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT o.customer_id, o.total_revenue, t.avg_resolution
FROM order_totals o
JOIN ticket_stats t ON o.customer_id = t.customer_id
```

Each CTE produces one row per customer before the join, so the final join is 1:1 and neither metric is inflated.

Option B is incorrect — both WHERE predicates apply correctly; SQL does not drop predicates on multiple date columns.

Option C is incorrect — MEDIAN also computes over duplicated rows. Changing the aggregation function does not remove the fan-out; it only changes which inflated statistic you compute.

Option D is incorrect — using a more granular join key (customer_id, order_date) joins orders to tickets sharing the exact same date, producing a different fan-out, not eliminating it. There is no fact-to-fact join key that prevents fan-out — only pre-aggregation does.
hints: How many rows does a JOIN of two tables produce when customer A has 10 rows in one fact and 5 rows in the other? What does SUM() compute over those 50 rows?
The fix is to reduce each fact to one row per customer *before* joining — not to change the join condition or the aggregation function.

title: Post-Acquisition Conformed Dimension: Resolving Overlapping Natural Keys
scenario_context: Company A acquires Company B. Both have a `customer` table with integer customer_id values starting at 1. Company A has 2M customer records (IDs 1–2,000,000); Company B has 800K records (IDs 1–800,000). The keys overlap: Company A customer_id=1001 and Company B customer_id=1001 are different people. The combined platform must serve cross-company analytics (e.g., combined revenue by customer segment) and must preserve the full order history from both companies. There is no requirement to identify shared customers across both companies — the two customer bases are completely disjoint.
description: Which dimensional modeling strategy correctly creates a unified conformed `dim_customer` without losing history or producing incorrect cross-company joins?
options: Generate new globally unique integer surrogate keys (1 through 2.8M) for all customers from both companies; maintain a natural_key_map table (global_customer_sk, source_system, original_customer_id) for reverse lookup; re-key all fact tables from both companies to use global_customer_sk; the conformed dimension has one row per unique (source, original_id) pair and the surrogate key is its primary key

Create a compound natural key combining source system prefix and original ID (e.g., 'A-1001' vs 'B-1001'); use this compound string as the dimension primary key; update all fact tables to use the compound string key; no surrogate key is needed because the compound key is globally unique

Keep two separate dimension tables (dim_customer_a and dim_customer_b); create a UNION ALL view dim_customer_combined with a source_system flag column; all analytics queries filter on source_system to prevent cross-company key collisions

Assign Company B all customer IDs above 2,000,000 by adding a 2,000,000 offset to all Company B customer IDs; update Company B's fact table rows to use offset IDs; use a single dim_customer table with no source_system tracking
explanation: Generating new globally unique surrogate keys is the canonical Data Vault and Kimball approach for merging dimension tables from sources with conflicting natural keys. The global surrogate key is a meaningless integer with no business semantics — this is the correct property of a surrogate key. The natural_key_map table preserves the ability to trace any global surrogate key back to its source system and original ID, which is essential for reverse lookups and audits. All fact tables from both companies are re-keyed once to use the new global surrogate keys. After migration, the conformed dimension is the single source of truth for all cross-company analytics. Option B (compound string key) uses a natural key as the dimension primary key. While globally unique, string join keys are slower than integer surrogate keys at scale, and the compound string encodes business meaning into the key — which creates maintenance issues if source system codes change. All fact tables still require re-keying (same effort as Option A with worse performance). Option C (UNION ALL view) is not a true conformed dimension — it is two separate dimensions in a view. Any cross-company analysis that needs to relate entities (e.g., comparing customer segments across both companies) requires a genuine unified dimension, not a union of two independent ones. Analytics that need consistent segment definitions across companies cannot be expressed correctly via a view union. Option D (offset hack) creates a fragile implicit convention: the offset assumes Company A will never grow beyond 2M customers; if it does, new keys from Company A collide with offset Company B keys. It also provides no source tracking — you cannot determine which company a customer came from by looking at the key alone.
hints: When two source systems have overlapping natural keys, what is the standard dimensional modeling pattern for creating a unified dimension with a stable primary key?

The natural_key_map table preserves the source system and original ID for every row in the conformed dimension. Why is this mapping necessary even after all fact tables have been re-keyed to global surrogate keys?

title: Semantic Layer: Deprecating a Certified Metric Without Breaking Downstream Consumers
description: A data platform certifies metrics in a semantic layer. The current certified metric `total_revenue` calculates gross revenue without deducting refunds. Finance needs a corrected metric `gross_revenue_net` that deducts refunds. 40 downstream consumers reference `total_revenue`: 18 Tableau workbooks, 12 dbt mart models, 7 Looker dashboards, and 3 Excel pivot tables connected via JDBC. The Finance team proposes renaming `total_revenue` to `gross_revenue_net` immediately. What is the correct deprecation and migration strategy?
options: Keep `total_revenue` active and simultaneously publish `gross_revenue_net` as a new certified metric; mark `total_revenue` as Deprecated in the semantic layer catalog with a clearly communicated 60-day sunset date; emit deprecation warnings to each consumer referencing the deprecated metric; notify all 40 consumer owners with a migration guide; remove `total_revenue` only after the sunset date has passed and all consumers have migrated or explicitly acknowledged

Rename `total_revenue` to `gross_revenue_net` immediately in the semantic layer; all 40 consumers receive a metric-not-found error on next refresh; send a migration announcement email with a 2-week update window; restore the metric name if any team cannot update in time

Make `total_revenue` a permanent alias pointing to `gross_revenue_net` in the semantic layer; all 40 consumers keep working under their existing name without changes; Finance uses the new canonical name; the alias is maintained indefinitely to avoid forced migration

Fork the semantic layer into a v1 namespace (containing `total_revenue`) and a v2 namespace (containing `gross_revenue_net`); consumers must explicitly opt into v2 on their own schedule; maintain v1 indefinitely so no consumer is ever forced to migrate
explanation: The standard certified metric deprecation lifecycle is: (1) publish the new metric alongside the old one — zero downtime for existing consumers; (2) mark the old metric as Deprecated with a sunset date — consumers are warned but not broken; (3) notify all consumer owners with a migration guide specific to their tool (different for Tableau, dbt, Looker, and Excel JDBC); (4) remove the deprecated metric only after the sunset date has passed and all consumers have confirmed migration. The 60-day window accounts for the slowest-moving consumer type (Excel JDBC connections often require manual updates by business users who may not monitor platform announcements). Option B (immediate rename) is not acceptable for a production platform: it breaks all 40 consumers simultaneously at next refresh, including Excel pivot tables and Tableau workbooks used by business stakeholders who cannot update in 2 weeks. Option C (permanent alias) is a governance antipattern: aliases create invisible dependencies in the catalog; when the underlying calculation changes in the future, both names silently reflect the change; consumers never learn the canonical metric name; and there is no migration signal in the catalog. Permanent aliases defeat the purpose of metric version management. Option D (forever v1 namespace) is equivalent: the v1 namespace must be maintained indefinitely with the same rigor as the v2 namespace — doubling maintenance — and consumers have no incentive to ever migrate, since nothing forces them to.
hints: Why is it important to publish `gross_revenue_net` before deprecating `total_revenue`, rather than renaming `total_revenue` in place?
A permanent alias gives consumers an existing name that keeps working. What does it NOT provide that a deprecation-with-sunset-date does provide?

title: Semi-Additive Fact Design for Balance with Period-Change Analytics
scenario_context: A bank's data warehouse has a daily account balance fact table (fact_account_balance_daily) with one row per (account_id, balance_date) and a `balance_amount` column. The Finance team needs two query patterns: (1) As-at balance: what was the total balance across all accounts on a specific date? Requires picking the balance for each account as of that date — summing across dates double-counts the same money. (2) Period change: what was the net change in total balance between two dates? Requires SUM(balance on date B) − SUM(balance on date A). A third team asks whether `balance_amount` can also support SUM queries for monthly interest accrual reporting across all accounts.
description: Which fact table design and column strategy correctly supports all three query patterns?
options: Keep the current snapshot (balance_amount per account per day) for pattern 1 and pattern 2 (computed as two single-date SUM queries subtracted); add a separate `daily_change` column to the same row capturing the day-over-day net balance movement; monthly interest accrual uses SUM(daily_change) within the month, which is fully additive — no double-counting because it sums changes, not balances

Replace balance_amount with a flow (change) column: store only the daily net change rather than the absolute balance; pattern 1 requires a running SUM of all daily changes from account inception to the target date; pattern 2 is a SUM of daily changes between the two dates; interest accrual is also a SUM of flows

Keep balance_amount as-is and add a query-time note in the data catalog that balance_amount is semi-additive: it can be summed across accounts but not across dates; train analysts to write date-filtered queries; the interest accrual team must use a different approach

Store a monthly rollup fact table (fact_account_balance_monthly) alongside the daily table: the monthly table has one row per (account_id, month) with a month_end_balance and monthly_change column; pattern 1 uses the daily table; pattern 2 and accrual use the monthly rollup table
explanation: Storing both the snapshot (balance_amount, semi-additive) and the flow (daily_change, fully-additive) in the same fact row is the standard Kimball recommendation for semi-additive measures that need to support multiple query patterns. Pattern 1 (as-at balance): uses `WHERE balance_date = :target_date` on balance_amount — a direct single-date read. Pattern 2 (period change): uses `SUM(daily_change) WHERE balance_date BETWEEN :date_a AND :date_b` — fully additive over the date range, no double-counting. Interest accrual: uses `SUM(daily_change) WHERE balance_date BETWEEN month_start AND month_end` — same fully-additive column. Option B (change-only) makes pattern 1 impractical at scale: every single-date as-at balance query requires a running SUM of all daily changes from account inception (potentially years of data) for every account in the result set. This is the defining weakness of a flow-only model. Option C (documentation only) does not add the daily_change column needed for interest accrual — the interest team must compute accrual from balance differences across two dates (two full-table reads) rather than summing a pre-computed flow column. Option D (monthly rollup table) solves the accrual problem but adds a second table to maintain in sync with the daily table; it is operationally more complex than adding one column to the existing row and does not reduce the daily table's query complexity.
hints: SUM(balance_amount) across multiple dates double-counts the same money. SUM(daily_change) across a date range is fully additive. Which design stores both so each query uses the correct column?
A flow-only table (Option B) stores only daily_change. What does a query for 'total account balance across all accounts on March 15th' require when there is no snapshot column?

title: Regulatory As-Of Reporting: When a Dimension Must Reconstruct Its Own Past State
scenario_context: A financial institution receives a regulatory audit request: 'Provide the complete customer risk classification table as it existed in your data warehouse on November 30th, 2023.' The current `dim_customer_risk` uses SCD Type 2. Investigation reveals that between December 1st and today, 12,000 rows were corrected — some with effective_from dates backdated into the November period. The current SCD Type 2 table, queried for November 30th using `effective_from <= '2023-11-30' AND effective_to > '2023-11-30'`, reflects the post-correction state. It cannot distinguish whether a row was in the database on November 30th or was added afterward with a backdated effective_from.
description: Which data warehouse design approach would have made this regulatory request answerable directly from the warehouse without relying on database backups or restore operations?
options: Bi-temporal design with system-time tracking: each SCD row carries `sys_start TIMESTAMP` and `sys_end TIMESTAMP` recording when the row was current in the database, independent of its effective_from/effective_to validity period. A November 30th audit query filters `WHERE '2023-11-30' BETWEEN sys_start AND sys_end` on the system-time axis, returning exactly the rows that were in the database on that date — including rows inserted before November 30th and excluding rows inserted or modified after.

Retain weekly full-dimension table snapshots in cold storage for 12 months; audit queries read the snapshot nearest to the target date; the SCD Type 2 logic remains unchanged and needs no modification for compliance reporting.

Implement a data quality rule that rejects any effective_from date more than 7 days in the past; this prevents backdated corrections from altering the apparent historical record, ensuring the current SCD Type 2 table always reflects what was entered contemporaneously with real-world events.

Add a `first_inserted_at TIMESTAMP` column to each SCD row recording when it was first created; audit queries filter WHERE first_inserted_at <= '2023-11-30' AND effective_to > '2023-11-30' to find rows that were present on that date and still valid in business time.
explanation: The audit request is a transaction-time (system-time) query: 'what did your database contain on November 30th?' — not 'what was true in the business on November 30th?' SCD Type 2's effective_from/effective_to is a valid-time model. A backdated correction added in December with effective_from in November looks identical in valid-time queries to a row that was genuinely present in November. Bi-temporal modeling adds a system-time axis (sys_start/sys_end) that records when each row was current in the database itself, independently of its business validity period. A corrected row added in December will have sys_start = December, regardless of its effective_from being backdated to November. The November 30th system-time query correctly excludes all December insertions and returns the exact set of rows that existed in the database that day. Option B (weekly snapshots) works operationally but is imprecise — the snapshot nearest to November 30th might be November 25th, missing 5 days of legitimate changes — and requires restoring potentially large table snapshots for a single query. Option C (reject backdated corrections) prevents future occurrences but provides no remedy for the 12,000 corrections already applied; it also prevents legitimate data corrections that have valid business reasons (late-arriving source data, discovered errors). Option D (first_inserted_at) captures row creation time but not modification time. When a correction closes an existing row by updating its effective_to, the original row's first_inserted_at is unchanged but its effective_to has been modified. The filter `WHERE first_inserted_at <= Nov 30 AND effective_to > Nov 30` cannot reconstruct the row's pre-modification effective_to value.
hints: The valid-time query returns what is believed to be true on November 30th based on current data. The audit request asks what was in the database on November 30th. Are these the same question?

A backdated correction inserted in December has effective_from in November. What should sys_start be for that corrected row — November (when the business fact was valid) or December (when it was entered into the system)?

title: Zero-Downtime Schema Migration for a High-Fan-Out Fact Table
scenario_context: A data platform must make two changes to `fact_events` (200M rows, consumed by 20 assets: 8 dbt models, 6 Tableau workbooks, 4 Python scripts, 2 R reports): (1) rename the column `evt_ts` to `event_timestamp`; (2) change `user_id` from BIGINT to VARCHAR to support a new UUID-based identity system. The platform team cannot take a multi-day downtime window — consumers cannot all update simultaneously, and some Tableau workbooks are maintained by business stakeholders who update on monthly schedules.
description: Which migration strategy achieves zero consumer downtime while giving all 20 assets a realistic path to the new schema?
options: Create a versioned view `fact_events_v2` that exposes the renamed column (`evt_ts AS event_timestamp`) and the cast user_id (`CAST(user_id AS VARCHAR) AS user_id`); keep the base `fact_events` table unchanged; communicate the migration path to all 20 consumer owners with a 60-day transition window; once all consumers point to fact_events_v2, rename the base table and update the view to a thin wrapper; no consumer experiences downtime during migration

Apply both changes to `fact_events` immediately; issue a migration announcement email with a 2-week update window; consumers that cannot update in time are temporarily broken until they apply the change; priority support is offered to Tableau workbook owners

Add `event_timestamp` as a new column alongside `evt_ts` and dual-write both during migration; add `user_id_str` as a new VARCHAR column alongside the existing BIGINT `user_id`; deprecate old columns after all consumers confirm migration; both old and new columns coexist for the duration of the migration window

Route all consumers through a semantic layer abstraction (dbt Semantic Layer or equivalent) that exposes `event_timestamp` and VARCHAR user_id as canonical field names regardless of the underlying physical column names; the physical migration happens transparently once all consumers adopt the semantic layer
explanation: A versioned view is the standard zero-downtime strategy for high-fan-out schema migrations. The view `fact_events_v2` exposes the new column name and cast type without any change to the underlying table. Consumers reading `fact_events` continue working unchanged; consumers reading `fact_events_v2` get the new schema immediately. Tableau workbooks maintained on monthly schedules can migrate during their next maintenance window — no urgency. Once all 20 consumers have migrated to fact_events_v2, the base table can be renamed and the view updated to a thin wrapper without any consumer impact. Option B (immediate breaking change) is incompatible with zero-downtime: it breaks all 20 consumers simultaneously. Tableau workbooks maintained by business stakeholders on monthly cycles will be broken for up to 4 weeks. Option C (dual columns) works but inflates the table schema: the table has both evt_ts and event_timestamp, plus user_id BIGINT and user_id_str VARCHAR, during the entire migration window. The dual-write requirement adds pipeline complexity and the risk of the two columns diverging. The view approach (Option A) achieves the same isolation without touching the base table. Option D (semantic layer) is a valid long-term architectural goal but it is not a migration strategy for a one-time schema change — it requires all 20 consumers to first adopt the semantic layer, which is itself a multi-month cross-team initiative and cannot be completed within a migration window.
hints: A database view can rename columns and cast types without modifying the underlying table. How does fact_events_v2 give all 20 consumers a zero-downtime migration path?
The 60-day window lets each consumer team update on their own schedule. What makes Option B (immediate rename) incompatible with a 20-team migration where some teams update monthly?

title: Intra-Day Periodic Snapshot: Granularity Trade-offs and Fact Table Design
description: A trading platform requires account balance snapshots at market open, midday, and market close (3 per trading day) rather than once daily. The current daily snapshot produces 50M rows/day for 50M accounts. Moving to 3 snapshots produces 150M rows/day and 37.5B rows/year. Three designs are being evaluated: (A) a single fact table with a snapshot_label column ('open', 'mid', 'close'); (B) three separate fact tables, one per snapshot time; (C) a change-event log plus reconstruction logic. Which design correctly balances query flexibility, storage, and cross-snapshot analytical clarity?
options: Design A (single table with snapshot_label): a compound primary key of (account_id, snapshot_timestamp) uniquely identifies each row; snapshot_label provides readability; date-level partitioning limits scan to one day's 150M rows; cross-snapshot comparison queries use `WHERE snapshot_label IN ('open', 'close')` in a single table scan without UNION ALL; the 3× row count is the unavoidable cost of 3× the granularity

Design B (three separate tables): each snapshot table is independently partitioned and sized; cross-snapshot comparison queries use UNION ALL; separate tables allow independent archiving if regulatory retention differs by snapshot type (e.g., close retained for 7 years, open and midday for 2 years)

Design C (change-event log + reconstruction): store only balance changes with a timestamp; reconstruct any snapshot time by summing changes from account inception to the target timestamp; storage grows only with real balance movements (many accounts are unchanged between open and close), dramatically reducing row count compared to storing three full snapshots per day

Design A with a twist: use a sparse representation where only accounts that changed between snapshots are stored; accounts with no intraday balance movement appear only at the end-of-day snapshot; the sparse design reduces 150M rows/day back toward 50M while retaining full intraday accuracy for active accounts
explanation: Design A (single table with snapshot_label) is the standard dimensional modeling approach for a fixed, known set of snapshot times per day. The advantages are clear: (1) cross-snapshot queries are single-table scans with a label filter — no UNION ALL, no JOIN complexity; (2) window functions like `LAG() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY snapshot_timestamp)` can compare consecutive snapshots in one pass; (3) date-level partitioning limits all analytical queries to the relevant day's rows; (4) the snapshot_label enables natural language filtering ('market_close') rather than timestamp arithmetic. The 3× row count is the direct, unavoidable cost of capturing 3× the granularity — it is not a design flaw. Design B (three tables) creates cross-snapshot query complexity: any analysis comparing open vs close balances requires UNION ALL or separate joins, complicating all analytical queries. The independent archiving argument is the strongest case for Design B, but regulatory retention differences between snapshot types are typically handled at the partition level within a single table (partitioning by snapshot_label OR by date + time range) rather than by splitting the table. Design C (change-event log) is storage-efficient but makes point-in-time balance queries expensive: 'what was the account balance at market open on March 15th?' requires summing all changes from account inception to market open for every account in the result — potentially years of changes. This is impractical for a 50M-account trading platform where open-balance queries are issued thousands of times per day. Design D (sparse representation) reduces storage at the cost of query complexity: analysts must now handle the distinction between 'row not present because unchanged' and 'row not present because error' — every balance query requires a COALESCE or gap-filling step, and analytical logic becomes significantly more complex.
hints: For a fixed set of known snapshot times (open, mid, close), what column distinguishes each snapshot type, and what compound key uniquely identifies each row?
Design C stores only changes between snapshots. What does a query for 'total balance across all 50M accounts at market open on March 15th' require when there is no snapshot column?

title: Bi-Temporal Modeling: When SCD Type 2 Cannot Reconstruct System State
scenario_context: A medical device company tracks device recall status using SCD Type 2. A status change from 'Active' to 'Under Review' was entered into the system on November 5th but was backdated to October 15th (the date the business decision was made). Regulatory auditors ask: 'What recall status did your system report for device D-441 on October 31st?' The current SCD Type 2 query for October 31st returns 'Under Review' (because the row has effective_from = October 15th). But the October monthly report sent to regulators on October 31st showed 'Active' — the 'Under Review' row hadn't been loaded yet.
description: Your current SCD Type 2 gives the wrong answer to the auditor's question because a backdated correction changes what history looks like today versus what the system contained at the time of the report. Which design pattern makes this audit question answerable directly from the data warehouse?
options: Add a second timestamp pair — sys_start and sys_end — to each SCD row, tracking when that row was current in the database independently of its effective_from/effective_to validity dates. A transaction-time query for 'what was in the system on October 31st' filters on `'2023-10-31' BETWEEN sys_start AND sys_end`, returning the 'Active' row that existed in the database before the November 5th load.

SCD Type 2 already answers this question: the 'Active' row has effective_from before October 31st, so the predicate WHERE effective_from <= '2023-10-31' AND effective_to > '2023-10-31' returns 'Active' — no design change is needed.

Add a date_loaded column to each SCD row. For the audit query, filter WHERE date_loaded <= '2023-10-31' AND effective_to > '2023-10-31' to find rows that were loaded before October 31st and still valid on that date.

Maintain a nightly snapshot of the full dimension table in a separate cold-storage schema. Audit queries read the snapshot for the relevant date rather than the live dimension, giving an exact replica of the system state on any past date.
explanation: Option A is bi-temporal modeling. SCD Type 2's effective_from/effective_to axis records when a fact was true in business reality (valid time). After the November 5th load, the SCD table shows: 'Active' from a prior date to October 14th, 'Under Review' from October 15th to present. A valid-time query for October 31st returns 'Under Review' — which reflects the backdated business fact but NOT what the system actually contained on October 31st when the report was generated. The system-time axis (sys_start/sys_end) records when each row was current in the database. The 'Under Review' row has sys_start = November 5th. A transaction-time query for October 31st excludes it and returns the 'Active' row (sys_start before October 31st, sys_end = November 5th when it was superseded). Option B is wrong: after the backdated load, 'Under Review' has effective_from = October 15th — the valid-time predicate for October 31st returns 'Under Review', not 'Active'. The current SCD gives the wrong audit answer. Option C is incomplete: date_loaded captures when a row was inserted, not when an existing row's effective_to was modified. When the correction was applied, the 'Active' row's effective_to was changed to October 14th — this modification happened after October 31st, but date_loaded reflects the original insert time. The audit filter cannot reconstruct the pre-modification table state from create timestamps alone. Option D (nightly snapshots) works operationally but is expensive, imprecise for intraday queries, and depends on backup infrastructure rather than query logic.
hints: After the November 5th backdated load, what does the valid-time predicate return for October 31st? Is that the answer the auditor needs?
Bi-temporal modeling has two independent time axes. Which axis tracks 'when was this row current in the database' independently of 'when was the business fact valid'?

title: Schema Evolution: Adding a Compliance Column to a Shared Dimension Under a Regulatory Deadline
scenario_context: A healthcare analytics platform has a shared `dim_patient` dimension (6M rows) consumed by three domains: Clinical (treatment analytics, 9 downstream dbt models), Finance (claim billing, 5 downstream models), and Research (de-identified nightly export to an academic partner governed by a data-sharing agreement). The governance team must add a `consent_level` column (values: 'full', 'limited', 'research_only', 'none') tracking patient data-sharing consent. Three constraints apply simultaneously: (1) consent data must be backfilled from a legacy paper-consent system — 85% coverage estimated over 3 months; (2) the Research export must begin filtering on consent_level within 30 days to meet a new regulatory requirement; (3) Clinical and Finance pipelines must not be disrupted during or after the migration.
description: Which schema evolution strategy satisfies all three constraints simultaneously, and why does each alternative violate at least one?
options: Add `consent_level` as NULL-allowed to `dim_patient` immediately; NULL = consent status pending backfill; deploy the Research export filter as `WHERE consent_level = 'research_only'` excluding NULLs by default (data-minimization default); Clinical and Finance are unaffected by a NULL-allowed column addition; backfill runs asynchronously over 3 months and the Research export population grows as records resolve.

Add `consent_level` as NOT NULL DEFAULT 'full' so the Research export can begin filtering within 30 days; the 15% of patients without backfill coverage default to 'full' consent; backfill corrects any inaccurate rows over 3 months; Clinical and Finance are unaffected by the column addition.

Block the Research export until the 3-month backfill reaches 100% coverage; add `consent_level` only after backfill completes; deploy all three domain changes simultaneously in a coordinated release window to guarantee a consistent view.

Create a separate `dim_patient_consent` table containing only patients with confirmed consent status; the Research export joins to it and excludes non-matching patients; Clinical and Finance continue using `dim_patient` unchanged; merge the consent table back into `dim_patient` after the backfill completes.
explanation: Option A satisfies all three constraints: (1) NULL-allowed column addition is backwards-compatible — Clinical and Finance models continue without modification; (2) the Research export filter `WHERE consent_level = 'research_only'` launches within 30 days, erring on the side of data minimization by excluding unknown-consent patients; (3) the backfill runs asynchronously and the export population grows as records resolve. This is the canonical approach to schema evolution under partial historical data availability. Option B fails on compliance: DEFAULT 'full' asserts full consent for 15% of patients whose status is unknown. 'full' consent means the patient has agreed to all data uses, including Research export. Defaulting to 'full' for unresolved patients could expose their data to the academic partner without authorization — a direct violation of healthcare consent regulations (HIPAA/GDPR). The correct default for unknown consent is absence of consent, not the broadest permission tier. Option C fails on the 30-day regulatory deadline: blocking the Research export for 3 months is not an option when a compliance date is fixed. Waiting for complete backfill before deploying defeats the incremental, non-disruptive principle of schema evolution. Option D adds complexity with no benefit over Option A: the outer join in the Research export achieves the same filtering as Option A's WHERE clause, but with a separate table to maintain and a 3-month merge operation that risks disrupting all three domains simultaneously — the opposite of a non-disruptive migration.
hints: Constraint 2 requires the Research export to start filtering within 30 days. Which options are immediately disqualified by that deadline?
If DEFAULT 'full' is used and a patient's consent later resolves to 'none', what was the data-sharing status of their records during the 3-month window when their row incorrectly showed 'full'?

title: Schema Evolution Governance: Breaking-Change Strategy for a High-Fan-Out Shared Dimension
description: A shared `dim_account` is consumed by 14 downstream assets across four business domains. The governance team evaluates three long-term strategies for handling breaking schema changes (column renames, type changes, removals) that occur 3–5 times per year: (A) Alias columns — add the new canonical name alongside the deprecated name, maintaining both indefinitely; (B) Versioned tables — publish `dim_account_v2` alongside `dim_account_v1`, deprecate v1 with a 90-day sunset; (C) Logical interface layer — a view or semantic API exposes the consumer-facing contract; breaking changes happen only in the physical table, with the interface remapping old names to new physical columns during a transition window. Which strategy scales best across a multi-year horizon with 3–5 breaking changes per year?
options: Strategy A (alias columns): each breaking change adds the new canonical name while retaining the deprecated name indefinitely; consumers never face forced migration and the dimension remains backward-compatible at all times. This is the lowest-risk strategy for a high-fan-out dimension with slow-moving consumers like Tableau workbooks and R scripts.

Strategy B (versioned tables): each breaking change gets its own physical version with a 90-day migration window; physical isolation ensures v1 consumers are protected from v2 changes; this provides the cleanest breaking-change governance because each version is an independently maintained asset.

Strategy C (logical interface layer): the physical table evolves freely; the interface enforces the consumer-facing contract; breaking changes are absorbed as temporary remappings in the interface and removed after migration — the physical table and interface stay lean because migration logic is never permanent.

None of these strategies is correct for a dimension with 14 consumers. The right governance model is a no-breaking-changes policy: once a column is published on a shared dimension, only new nullable columns or new attribute values may be added; renames, type changes, and deletions are prohibited.
explanation: Strategy C is correct for a high-fan-out dimension with frequent breaking changes. The interface layer absorbs each change as a temporary mapping that is removed after consumers migrate — keeping both the physical table and the interface lean over time. Strategy A (alias columns indefinitely) accumulates technical debt at the rate of the breaking-change frequency: 3–5 per year over 5 years produces 15–25 permanently maintained alias columns. With 14 consumers, aliases are never safely removed (someone always depends on the old name), and the dimension becomes a museum of deprecated column names. No analyst can tell which columns are canonical without reading documentation that itself drifts. Strategy B (versioned tables) fails because each version requires the same full operational rigor as the original: matching SCD logic, partitioning strategy, refresh cadences, and lineage tracking. With 14 consumers across 4 domains moving to v2 at different paces, both v1 and v2 must be fully maintained for the entire 90-day window — and in practice, some consumer never migrates. At 3–5 breaking changes per year, table proliferation becomes unsustainable. Strategy D overstates the constraint. Breaking changes — renames for correctness, type changes for precision, removals of deprecated attributes — are sometimes necessary. A blanket prohibition forces teams to maintain semantically incorrect columns indefinitely.
hints: If Strategy A never removes deprecated column names (because some consumer always depends on the old name), what does `dim_account` look like after 5 years of 3–5 breaking changes per year?
With Strategy B and 14 consumers across 4 domains each migrating to v2 on different schedules, how many versions of `dim_account` might coexist at once, and who maintains SCD correctness for each?

title: M1 Follow-up: Procedure-Grain Fact at 200M Rows — Aggregate Fact Design Under Scale
scenario_context: Following M1: the hospital system expands to 50 hospitals, growing `fact_procedures` to 200M rows per year. Executive dashboards — which only need unique patient counts and total revenue by department and quarter — now take 4–8 minutes. The data engineering team evaluates: (A) add a visit-level aggregate fact alongside the procedure fact, (B) replace `fact_procedures` with a pre-aggregated monthly rollup and archive the granular data, (C) partition `fact_procedures` by hospital and route dashboard queries to hospital-specific partitions.
description: Which strategy addresses the performance problem at 200M rows without sacrificing the procedure-level flexibility the clinical analytics team requires?
options: Add `fact_visit_summary` at the visit level (total_revenue, unique patient_key) refreshed nightly alongside `fact_procedures`. Executive dashboards query fact_visit_summary; clinical analysts who need procedure-type breakdown continue querying fact_procedures. Both facts share conformed dimensions and are produced by the same ETL pipeline, preventing metric divergence.

Replace `fact_procedures` with a monthly rollup table (one row per department × month with pre-aggregated unique patient count and total revenue) and archive the granular data to cold storage. Executive dashboards become instant; procedure-level queries access the archive only for audits.

Partition `fact_procedures` by hospital_key and year. Dashboard queries filter on hospital subsets, reducing each scan to 1/50 of the full table. No structural change to the fact is needed; partitioning is a transparent optimization.

Add a database-level materialized view with pre-aggregated unique patient counts and total revenue by department and quarter over `fact_procedures`. Redirect the BI tool to the materialized view; procedure-level detail remains in the base fact.
explanation: Option A is correct: the aggregate fact pattern (also called aggregate navigator in Kimball) places a pre-aggregated fact alongside the granular fact. The visit-level aggregate (fact_visit_summary) is small and fast for executive queries; the procedure-level fact remains available for clinical analytics. Both facts share conformed dimensions and are produced by the same ETL, so department and revenue definitions cannot diverge. BI tools that support aggregate awareness route dashboard queries to fact_visit_summary automatically. Option B (replace + archive) destroys analytical access to procedure-level data for all non-audit purposes. Archiving 200M rows to cold storage means any procedure-type revenue breakdown, clinical quality study, or readmission analysis requires expensive cold-storage retrieval — abandoning the analytical investment made in the procedure-level design. Option C (hospital partitions) reduces scan size when filtering by hospital, but a dashboard that aggregates all 50 hospitals still touches all 50 partitions. Partitioning is a storage strategy, not an aggregation optimizer; it does not eliminate the 200M-row aggregation cost for company-wide dashboard queries. Option D (materialized view) is operationally viable but has limitations: materialized view refresh lag may produce stale dashboards; engine-specific syntax creates lock-in; and the view lacks the lineage transparency of an explicitly documented aggregate fact with its own tests and documentation.
hints: A dashboard that aggregates all 50 hospitals' patient counts and revenue by quarter is doing fundamentally different work from a clinical analyst examining procedure codes. Does serving both from one 200M-row table make sense, or does each need a purpose-built surface?

If an aggregate fact and the granular fact are built from the same ETL pipeline and share the same conformed dimensions, what ensures that a quarterly revenue number from the aggregate fact matches the same query against the granular fact?

title: M1 Follow-up: Deduplicating Source Procedure Rows Without Losing Legitimate Repeats
scenario_context: Following M1: the hospital's operational system has a known ETL bug — under high load, a procedure is occasionally inserted twice into the source (same patient, visit, procedure code, amount, and timestamp). The ETL team detects this in 0.3% of procedure records across the 200M-row fact. However, some patients legitimately receive the same procedure twice in one visit (bilateral knee injections, two blood draws). The team evaluates: (A) SELECT DISTINCT on the full natural key set in staging, (B) unique constraint on (patient_key, visit_key, procedure_code), (C) flag-and-keep both rows with an is_suspect boolean.
description: Which strategy correctly eliminates system-bug duplicates without discarding legitimate repeated procedures, and why do the other two fail on either false positives or false negatives?
options: SELECT DISTINCT on the full natural key (patient_id, visit_id, procedure_code, procedure_timestamp, amount) in staging. True system-bug duplicates are identical on every column including timestamp and amount; legitimate repeated procedures differ on at least one column (different timestamp, different line item amount). Full-column dedup eliminates bug duplicates without touching legitimate repeats.

Add a unique constraint on (patient_key, visit_key, procedure_code). Any second row with the same three-value combination is rejected at load time and logged. This eliminates both exact duplicates and billing errors while producing an audit trail of all discarded rows.

Keep both rows and set is_suspect = TRUE on the duplicate. Analysts who need accurate procedure counts filter WHERE NOT is_suspect. The flag preserves an audit trail for the source system team to investigate and never discards data from the fact.

Apply a deduplication window: for any (patient_id, visit_id, procedure_code) combination, retain only the first occurrence within a 24-hour window. This handles both exact duplicates and near-duplicates where timestamps differ by seconds due to system clock skew.
explanation: Option A is correct. The system bug produces truly identical rows on every column — same patient, visit, code, timestamp, and amount. SELECT DISTINCT on the full natural key set removes exactly these rows. Legitimate repeated procedures (bilateral injections, two blood draws) differ on at least one column: they have different procedure line IDs, different timestamps (performed minutes apart), or different amounts (left vs right knee may have different billing codes). Full-column dedup is surgical — it eliminates only the impossible-in-reality exact replicas. Option B (unique constraint on three columns) is too broad: it rejects a patient who legitimately receives the same procedure type twice in one visit (bilateral injection = two rows with the same patient_key, visit_key, and procedure_code but different timestamps and amounts). This creates false negatives — real clinical events discarded from the fact. Option C (flag-and-keep) pollutes the fact with known-bad data and forces every downstream analyst to apply the filter WHERE NOT is_suspect. If any consumer forgets the filter — a new team member, an ad hoc query, a third-party BI tool — their procedure counts and revenue totals are wrong by 0.3%. The correct design is clean facts, not flagged facts. Option D (24-hour window by code) creates the same false negative problem as Option B: a patient receiving two bilateral injections in one visit, 30 minutes apart, shares the same (patient, visit, code) and falls within the 24-hour window. The first occurrence is kept; the second is discarded incorrectly.
hints: A bilateral knee injection for a patient produces two procedure rows — same patient, same visit, same procedure code — but with different timestamps (left knee at 10:00, right knee at 10:45) and possibly different amounts. How does a unique constraint on (patient_key, visit_key, procedure_code) treat these two rows?

A system-bug duplicate has the same patient, visit, code, timestamp, and amount as the original. A legitimate repeated procedure has the same patient, visit, and code, but a different timestamp and possibly a different amount. Which deduplication key distinguishes the two cases correctly?

title: M2 Follow-up: Arbitrary-Date Balance Query at 500M Rows — Pre-Aggregation vs Partitioning
scenario_context: Following M2: the bank's `fact_balance_snapshot` has grown to 500M rows (10M accounts × 50 days of history). A regulatory requirement demands: 'Total balance across all accounts on any arbitrary past date — response under 5 seconds.' Full-table scans take 45–120 seconds. The team evaluates: (A) a pre-aggregated daily total table (`fact_daily_balance_total` — one row per date, total_balance), (B) partitioning `fact_balance_snapshot` by snapshot_date to reduce per-query scan size, (C) a running balance ledger with current account balances updated nightly.
description: Which strategy definitively satisfies the 5-second SLA for arbitrary-date balance queries while preserving account-level access for other analytical needs?
options: Add `fact_daily_balance_total` (one row per date, pre-aggregated total_balance across all accounts), refreshed nightly from `fact_balance_snapshot` by the same ETL pipeline. The arbitrary-date query becomes a single-row point lookup: `SELECT total_balance WHERE snapshot_date = target_date` — sub-second regardless of account count. The account-level snapshot is retained for per-account analytics.

Partition `fact_balance_snapshot` by snapshot_date. An arbitrary-date query scans only one partition (~10M rows instead of 500M). Partition pruning reduces the scan from 500M to ~10M rows — fast enough to meet the 5-second SLA without a separate aggregate table.

Maintain a running balance ledger (one row per account, current balance only), updated nightly. The arbitrary-date query joins the ledger to the snapshot to reconstruct historical totals for any past date.

Add a columnar index on snapshot_date and balance to `fact_balance_snapshot`. An index-assisted scan for a single date retrieves only the balance column across all accounts for that date, reducing I/O to the minimum needed for a SUM.
explanation: Option A is correct. Pre-aggregating the daily total into a one-row-per-date table collapses 500M rows to ~365 rows per year for the specific query pattern. The response time for `SELECT total_balance WHERE snapshot_date = target_date` is sub-second — a single-row lookup against a tiny table, with no scan of the 500M-row account-level fact. Both tables are maintained by the same ETL pipeline, ensuring the daily total is always consistent with account-level detail. Option B (date partitioning) is a partial improvement but insufficient. Each date partition has 10M rows (10M accounts). A SUM(balance) across 10M rows with disk I/O still takes 3–15 seconds depending on cluster resources — the SLA is not reliably met. Partitioning reduces scan size but does not eliminate the aggregation computation. Option C (running ledger) does not retain historical state.
